It says a citywide replacement would need a separate budget decision after accessibility and operations review. None of the listed prices is a contract award, and the file contains no signed vendor selection, purchase order, rollout calendar, or projected benefit calculation. The pilot's measured match rate may be relevant to later deliberation, but it neither authorizes procurement nor predicts citywide savings.

unit_ledger.text: The pilot established that 71% of 4,860 included visits reached a desk within the displayed wait band, with results ranging from 66% to 75% across three branches [S1][S2].
It did not establish that the display improved service relative to no display, reduced abandonment, worked equally well for all groups, or would produce similar citywide results [S1][S2].
The evidence supports further controlled and accessibility testing, but not citywide procurement or deployment at this stage [S1][S2]. (judgment)
| Wait-band matching | 71% overall; branch range 66%–75% [S1][S2] | Included visits only; the supplied excerpts do not establish why branch match rates differed. |
| Operational stability | 58 staff-recorded corrections [S1][S2] | Correction labels were not independently audited [S2] |
| Accessibility | 15 of 18 volunteer sessions announced the band [S2] | Small simulated review; population performance across devices, languages, and assistive technologies is unknown [S2] |
| Causal benefit | Unknown [S1][S2] | No before-period comparison, randomization, or alternative-display comparison [S1][S2] |
| Citywide readiness | Unknown and unapproved [S2] | No approved budget, vendor selection, purchase order, rollout date, or projected benefit calculation [S2] |
The pilot ran from 2026-06-01 through 2026-08-15 in three municipal library branches [S1].
Its 4,860 included visits excluded appointments, school groups, and days when the ticket printer was offline [S1][S2].
Across those visits, 71% reached a desk within the displayed wait band, and the reported branch range was 66% to 75% [S1][S2].
The display communicated a band rather than an exact wait in minutes [S1].
The 71% result describes agreement between the displayed band and recorded desk time, not universal accuracy or improvement caused by the display [S1][S2].
Differences among branch configurations likewise cannot be interpreted causally because the results were unadjusted and no causal experiment was conducted [S1][S2].
Staff recorded 58 display corrections: 21 after a sick call, 17 after a late-opening program, 12 after a ticket-printer restart, and 8 with only a short free-text description [S1][S2].
These staff-entered classifications were not independently audited [S2].
An accessibility review of 18 volunteer sessions found that 15 announced the band through the configured screen reader [S2].
Two sessions involved browser-extension conditions, and one involved a changed display language without a translated label [S2].
The materials contain no pre-display comparison, visitor randomization, comparison of alternative displays, or estimate of staffing-demand effects [S1][S2].
They also do not establish that queue abandonment declined [S1][S2].
The appendix provides anonymized counts but not individual visitor demographics [S1].
Consequently, the evidence cannot establish equal usefulness across visitor groups [S1][S2].
Citywide replacement would require a separate budget decision [S2].
The materials contain no contract, signed vendor selection, purchase order, rollout calendar, approved citywide benefit estimate, or deployment authorization [S2].
The pilot can inform later deliberation, but its match rate neither predicts citywide savings nor authorizes procurement [S1][S2].
The supplied materials do not approve a rollout date or citywide deployment [S2].
No source in the supplied record directly contradicts the reported pilot measurements [S1][S2].
However, S2 is truncated, so omitted portions could not be reviewed here [S2].
The accessibility sessions were simulated, reviewer-observed, and recruited through a local advisory group rather than designed as representative population testing [S2].
The supplied excerpts do not measure whether visitors abandoned the queue less often [S1].
These omissions limit causal, equity, accessibility, and economic conclusions without negating the observed match rate [S1][S2].
1. Run a pre-specified follow-up that includes a comparison condition and measures abandonment, staffing demand, and visitor understanding [S1][S2]. (judgment)
2. Test translated labels across representative devices, languages, browser settings, and assistive technologies while retaining a staffed alternative during evaluation [S2]. (judgment)
3. Define an outcome threshold and require accessibility, operations, budget, and projected-benefit reviews before any procurement decision [S2]. (judgment)
